title: Phase 1 of moving rules from prose into code: a checked inventory of every firstmate rule, and parser-based test sweeps in place of brittle text sweeps
public_title: Check firstmate rules in code and replace brittle test sweeps
acceptance: Why. The firstmate skill file, `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md`, is about 103 KB of prose. It holds roughly 160 sentences that state a rule with the words must, never, do not, don't or always. Nobody can tell from the file which of those rules a program already checks, which ones a program could check, and which ones need judgement. The captain wants rules moved into code where possible, and the skill file shrunk below 25 KB without losing a rule. That is too large for one pull request, so this task is phase 1: it builds the rule inventory and replaces the brittle test sweeps. Phase 2, a separate follow-up task, rewrites the skill file.

Why the sweeps. Some tests decide what counts as code by reading raw text, and they break when someone formats code differently. In `tests/decide.test.sh` (function `code()`, about line 1058), only lines that start with `#` or `//` count as comments, so a Python docstring (the string at the top of a module, class or function) that mentions `bin/fm.sh` counts as a call to it. The same file (about lines 1136 to 1160) accepts a Herdr guard only as a line that starts at column 0: `^export HERDR_ENV=0` for shell and `^os\.environ\['HERDR_ENV'\] = '0'` for Python. A Herdr guard is a line that turns off the Herdr terminal integration, so a test suite cannot raise a real captain card by accident. The column-0 rule rejects `set -e; export HERDR_ENV=0`, which is a real guard, and accepts an unindented export inside an `if` block, which is not a guard. Two test helpers, `tests/lib/config-modules.sh` (lines 4 to 10) and `tests/lib/project-storage.sh` (lines 6 to 15), copy a hand-written list of `bin/lib` modules into test fixtures. When a pull request adds an import to one of those modules, about 45 suites that use the helpers fail with an import error far from the cause.

Inventory file. A new file, `skills/firstmate/rule-inventory.json`, lists the rules of `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md`. It is a JSON object with `version` set to 1, a `rules` array and a `retired` array. Each entry in `rules` has these fields: `id` (a rule ID of the form `R-` plus three or more digits, for example `R-001`), `file` (the repository path of the prose that holds the rule, `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` for every entry in this phase), `heading` (the exact text, without the leading `#` marks, of the nearest Markdown heading of any level above the rule, or the empty string for a rule that comes before the first heading), `quote` (a verbatim part of the rule sentence, at least 20 characters long), and `class`. The nearest heading can be the top-level `# Firstmate startup contract` heading (line 6), because the skill file has rules before its first `##` heading, for example at lines 13, 35 and 42.

Classes. The `class` field has one of three values. `enforced` means a check in code already refuses a breach of the rule; the entry then has an `evidence` list of one or more objects `{file, text}`, where `text` is the exact assertion message or refusal message of that check. `enforceable` means no check exists yet but a program could check the rule; the entry then has a `proposal` field of one or two sentences that describe the structured check to build. `judgement` means the rule needs a person's or a model's judgement and stays prose; it needs no extra field.

Inventory content. The worker classifies every rule sentence of `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` as defined in the coverage requirement below, one entry per rule, including the rules under the top-level heading. A sentence that holds two separate rules may get two entries with two different quotes. The inventory stores no line numbers, so an edit elsewhere in the file cannot break it. When an entry is removed, its ID moves to `retired` and is not used again. The checker sees only the current tree, not earlier versions of the file, so it enforces only that no ID is in both `rules` and `retired`; that a removed ID was retired and never reused is a rule for authors and reviewers, and this phase does not check it by program.

Checker. A new module, `bin/lib/fm_rules.py`, has one command, `python3 bin/lib/fm_rules.py check --root <dir>`. It validates the inventory against the tree at `<dir>`, prints one line per problem, exits 0 when there is none and 1 when there is any, and writes no file. For each uncovered rule sentence it also prints a ready stub entry as one line of JSON, with the heading, a quote and an empty class, so the author can paste it into the inventory and fill in the class.

Check, entries. `check` refuses an inventory that cannot be read: a missing file, invalid JSON, a top level that is not an object, `version` not equal to the integer 1, or `rules` or `retired` missing or not an array. Such a refusal names the inventory file, and the check stops there. Otherwise it checks each entry and refuses: an entry that is not an object; a missing field or a field of the wrong type (`id`, `file`, `heading` and `quote` must be strings, `evidence` a list of objects with string `file` and `text`, `proposal` a non-empty string); an `id` with the wrong form; a `quote` shorter than 20 characters; two entries with the same `id`; a `retired` item that is not a well-formed ID, or that appears twice; an `id` that is also in `retired`; a `class` that is not one of the three values; an `enforced` entry with no `evidence`; and an `enforceable` entry with no `proposal`. Each of these refusals names the rule ID; when an entry has no valid ID, it names the entry's position instead, for example `rules[12]` for an entry and `retired[3]` for a malformed or repeated item of `retired`.

Check, quotes. For each entry, `check` collapses runs of whitespace to one space in both the quote and the file, then requires the quote to appear exactly once in `file`, inside the section of `heading`. A section starts at its heading line and ends at the next heading of any level; the empty heading means the text before the first heading. If two headings have the same text, the quote must sit in exactly one of their sections. A quote that is missing, appears twice, or sits under another heading is refused, and the line names the rule ID and the reason.

Check, evidence. For each `evidence` object of an `enforced` entry, `check` requires that `file` exists under `<dir>` and that `text` appears in it outside a comment. For a Python file, the text must sit inside a string token, found with Python's `tokenize` module. For any other file, it must sit on a line that does not start, after spaces, with `#` or `//`. Evidence found only in a comment is refused, and the line names the rule ID and the evidence file. This proves only that the cited message exists in code; whether that check really enforces the rule is the reviewer's judgement.

Check, coverage. `check` reads `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` and finds every rule sentence. A rule sentence is a sentence outside a fenced code block that contains one of the whole words must, never, always, `do not` or `don't`, in any letter case. Sentences are found by joining each paragraph and each list item onto one line, then splitting after `.`, `;`, `?` or `!` when whitespace and an upper-case letter, a backtick or an opening bracket follow. A rule sentence is covered when the quote of at least one entry appears in it. Each uncovered sentence is refused with the file, the line where the sentence starts and the sentence text, followed by its stub entry as described in the checker requirement.

Gate stage. `bin/ci.sh` gains a stage named `rule inventory` in its fast group (the group that `--stage fast` runs, between about lines 580 and 1215). It runs `fm_rules.py check` from the same `bin/lib` directory as `ci.sh`, against the tree that `ci.sh` judges (`FM_ROOT`). When the stage passes, it prints one pass line with the number of rules in each class. When the check refuses, the stage turns the gate red and prints each refusal line. The stage is reported as skipped, without starting the checker and without reading any file of the tree, in two cases: the tree has no `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md`, or `FM_EXTERNAL=1` is set (a gate run for an external project, whose text must never be printed into this repository's gate output).

Source reader. A new test helper, `tests/lib/source_scan.py`, reads a source file the way its language parser reads it. Its `code <file>` command prints the file without comments. For a Python file, it parses the file with the `ast` module, drops docstrings, and prints the result of `ast.unparse`; other string literals stay, because a string can be a real command argument. For a shell file, it asks bash itself to parse the file. First it runs `<bash> -n <file>`; a file that fails this syntax check makes the command exit non-zero and name the file, and it is never read as plain text instead. Then it wraps the file in a function definition with `eval` and prints `declare -f` of that function. Bash drops comments, keeps quoted strings and heredoc bodies, and puts each command on its own line with its nesting shown by indentation. Because the file passed the syntax check on its own, the wrapper cannot be closed early by the file's text, so this defines the function and runs none of the file. As a second barrier, the parsing bash runs with an empty environment, `PATH` set to an empty directory, and no startup files (`--noprofile --norc`).

Guard detection. `tests/lib/source_scan.py` also has `py-guard <file>` and `sh-guard <file>`. `py-guard` succeeds when a statement of the Python module body itself (not inside an `if`, `try`, `with`, loop, function or class) assigns the string `'0'` to `os.environ['HERDR_ENV']`, in any quoting or spacing. `sh-guard` succeeds when the `declare -f` output has a line at the top indentation level that is a single simple `export` command setting `HERDR_ENV=0`. Each command of a `;`-separated line gets its own output line, so `set -e; export HERDR_ENV=0` counts. An export that is part of a list joined by `&&` or `||`, a pipeline, a background command (`&`), a subshell `( ... )` or a group `{ ...; }`, or that sits inside a function, `if`, `case` or loop, does not count, because it may not run or may not change the shell that runs the rest of the suite.

Bash selection. `code` and `sh-guard` take a required `--bash <path>` argument naming the bash that parses the file. The calling suites pass `"$BASH"`, the bash that runs them, so the helper gives the same answer as the suite's own shell: bash 3.2 on macOS and bash 5.2 on the Linux runner. Without `--bash`, or with a path that is not an executable file, the helper exits non-zero; it never picks another bash by itself.

Decide suite sweep. In `tests/decide.test.sh`, function `code()` (about line 1058) uses `source_scan.py code` for `.sh` and `.py` files. For TypeScript files it keeps today's rule of dropping lines that start with `#` or `//`, because the Python standard library has no TypeScript parser. It still follows sourced `tests/lib/*.sh` helpers and the `from herdr import` helper, as today. The guard check (about lines 1136 to 1160) uses `py-guard` and `sh-guard` in place of the column-0 patterns. The check for the shared loop that unsets every `HERDR_*` variable, and the check for a suite's own `herdr` stub first on `PATH`, stay as they are.

Decide suite assertions. Every existing assertion name in the sweep stays. The four Python guard assertions (about lines 1141 to 1144) keep their names; an input that is not valid Python on its own, such as a single indented line, is replaced by an equivalent complete program, such as the same assignment inside `if FLAG:`. The sweep still finds `tests/e2e-loop.test.sh` and `tests/selfupdate.test.sh` as suites that reach a card, and still reports `bin/fm.sh bin/lib/fm_autopilot_loop.py ` as the only card raisers.

Gate suite sweep. `tests/gate.test.sh` has the same kind of comment-stripping helper (`code()`, about line 476), used to find suites that run the real gate. For `.sh` and `.py` files it uses `source_scan.py code`. For other files, such as `board/server.ts` and `board/public/index.html`, and for its own extension-less comment sample, it keeps today's `sed` rule, so the assertion named 'a comment line, a trailing comment and an HTML comment are not code' keeps its input and its expected output.

Module registry. A new file, `tests/lib/fixture-modules.json`, declares the module sets that test fixtures copy. It has two sets: `config` (today's five files in `tests/lib/config-modules.sh`) and `project-storage` (the `config` set plus today's files in `tests/lib/project-storage.sh`: `fm-config.sh`, `fm-emit.sh` and `fm-herdr.py` from `bin/`, and the `bin/lib` files that helper copies, including `fm_gates.json`). Paths are repository paths. A file under `bin/lib/` lands in `<dest>/lib/`, and any other file under `bin/` lands in `<dest>/`, exactly as today.

Import closure. A new helper, `tests/lib/fixture_modules.py`, copies a set into a destination. It copies every declared file, plus every `bin/lib` Python module that a copied Python file imports when it loads. Such an import is an `import` or `from ... import` statement that the `ast` module finds outside any function body, including inside a top-level `if` or `try`. The helper follows those imports transitively. It does not follow imports inside a function body (lazy imports), so code that falls back when an optional module is missing keeps behaving as it does today. Its commands are `list <set>`, which prints the repository paths it would copy, and `copy <set> <dest>`.

Fixture helpers keep their interface. `config_modules_fixture <dest>` and `project_storage_fixture <dest>` keep their names, arguments and destination layout, and call `tests/lib/fixture_modules.py copy`. One existing rule stays: `project_storage_fixture` does not overwrite `<dest>/lib/fm_binding.py` when that file already exists, because `tests/lib/binding-fixture.sh` installs a stub with that name. The registry records this as a `keep_existing` list on the `project-storage` set. None of the callers changes. The callers are 45 suites under `tests/` (for example `tests/board.test.sh`, `tests/merge.test.sh` and `tests/ci-lints.test.sh`), plus `tests/lib/review.sh`, `tests/lib/card_refs.py` (about line 630) and `tests/stacking_cases.py` (about line 54).

Skill pointer. In `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md`, the section 'Spec preflight before dispatch and repin' gets one paragraph after the paragraph that starts 'Every task changing a validation rule' (about line 1489). It says that `skills/firstmate/rule-inventory.json` lists every rule sentence of the skill file, that the gate refuses a rule sentence with no entry, and that a spec which adds or rewords such a sentence lists `skills/firstmate/rule-inventory.json` in its scope and adds or updates the entry. That paragraph is itself a rule sentence and has its own inventory entry. No other text in the skill file changes in this phase.

Design. `design/design.md` section 10 (CI, about line 2900) gets a new subsection at the end of the section, before section 11, titled 'Rule inventory (T-279)'. It describes the inventory file, the three classes, the `rule inventory` stage of the fast group, what the stage refuses, and that phase 2 rewrites the skill file against this inventory.

Tests, new behaviour. A new suite, `tests/rule-inventory.test.sh`, runs the repository's `bin/ci.sh --stage fast` with `FM_ROOT` set to a fixture tree that it builds from small files in `tests/fixtures/rule-inventory/` (a short skill file with a top-level heading, `##` and `###` headings, a rule before the first heading and a fenced code block, plus an inventory and an evidence file). It never calls `fm_rules.py` directly. On the base, `bin/ci.sh` has no rule inventory stage, so each assertion fails because the stage's lines or exit status are missing, which is a behavioural failure and not a missing file. Named assertions: a matching inventory gives the pass line with the class counts, and the gate exits 0 in that fixture, where every other fast stage passes or skips; the same fixture with one planted rule sentence and no entry makes the gate exit non-zero and prints the sentence's line number, its text and its stub entry; rules before the first heading and under the top-level heading are covered by entries; a quote that is missing, appears twice or sits under the wrong heading is refused with its rule ID; an `enforced` entry whose evidence file is missing, or whose text appears only in a comment, is refused; each schema refusal in the entries requirement is refused, including an entry without an ID named as `rules[<n>]` and a malformed `retired` item named as `retired[<n>]`; the word must inside a fenced code block is not a rule sentence; an inventory or evidence `file` that is absolute, contains `..`, or is a symbolic link pointing outside the tree is refused; a tree without `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` reports the stage as skipped; and with `FM_EXTERNAL=1` the stage reports skipped and prints no text of the fixture's skill file.

Tests, tooling. Two new suites test the new test helpers. They pass on both the base and the head, because the helpers are test files, which the fail-first check keeps on the base; they are not the fail-first evidence. `tests/source-scan.test.sh` checks that `code` drops a Python docstring that mentions `bin/fm.sh` but keeps a string argument with the same text; drops a shell trailing comment and keeps a heredoc body; finds `set -e; export HERDR_ENV=0` as a top-level shell guard; rejects an export inside `if` or inside a function; finds a top-level Python guard written with double quotes and no spaces; rejects one inside `if FLAG:`; rejects an export joined by `&&` or `||`, in a pipeline, in the background, in a subshell or in a group; exits non-zero naming the file for a file that does not parse; exits non-zero without `--bash` or with a non-executable `--bash`; uses the given bash, shown by a logging stub bash that then runs the real one; and runs none of the scanned file, shown by a marker file that stays absent after scanning a file whose top level runs `touch <marker>` and after scanning a file that tries to close the wrapper early with `}` followed by `touch <marker>`. `tests/fixture-modules.test.sh` checks that, in a copied set, every copied Python module imports cleanly with only the destination on `sys.path`; that a module added to a member's top-level imports, in a temporary copy of `bin/`, is copied without a registry edit; that a lazy import is not followed; and that an existing `fm_binding.py` stub is kept.

Tests, regressions. These existing suites must pass and keep every assertion name: `tests/decide.test.sh` and `tests/gate.test.sh` (with the input change to the four Python guard assertions described above), and every suite that calls `config_modules_fixture` or `project_storage_fixture`, without edits to those callers.

Rollout and in-flight work. No record, pin, event, schema or stored-format change. Existing pins and SPEC-OK receipts stay valid for exactly the bytes they bind and nothing more. Once this merges, any pull request that adds or rewords a rule sentence in `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` turns the fast stage red until it adds or updates an inventory entry. That pull request's task then needs `skills/firstmate/rule-inventory.json` in its scope, which means the normal path for a scope change: an amended spec, a fresh exact-byte preflight, an authorized repin to a new pin version, and only then the next round; the old pin and receipt stay on record unchanged. These open pull requests edit the skill file today and may be affected: T-256 (#256), T-260 (#257), T-244 (#258), T-271 (#259), T-270 (#260), T-272 (#261) and T-262 (#248). Tests that prove each step: the planted-sentence assertion of `tests/rule-inventory.test.sh` proves the refusal and the stub. A new regression test, `test_scope_widening_needs_authorized_repin` in `tests/lib/spec_pins_cases.py` (run by `tests/spec-pins.test.sh`), proves the transition with the existing pin code and no production change: a change that adds a file outside the pinned scope is refused with `out of scope: <path>`; after an amended spec that adds the file to scope is committed and an authorized repin creates pin version 2, the same change passes the scope check; and pin version 1 stays on disk unchanged. It passes on base and head, because pin behaviour does not change. Two existing tests cover the other steps and are not edited: `test_repin_and_existing_inflight_pin_need_new_preflight` in `tests/lib/spec_preflight_cases.py` (changed bytes need a new preflight) and `test_changed_snapshot_and_authorized_repin` in `tests/lib/spec_pins_cases.py` (authorized version creation that keeps the old pin).

Language and privacy. The gate output and the inventory are English only, like the rest of `bin/ci.sh`; no board text or i18n dictionary changes. The checker reads only files inside the tree it judges: every `file` in the inventory and its evidence must be a relative path without `..`, and its resolved path, after following symbolic links, must stay inside `<dir>`; anything else is refused without being read. The inventory quotes only `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md`, which is generic, and names no external project or private path. With `FM_EXTERNAL=1` the stage skips, as stated in the gate stage requirement.

Out of scope, phase 2. A follow-up task rewrites `skills/firstmate/SKILL.md` into judgement principles plus pointers, below 25 KB. It moves each removed rule into a versioned reference file under `skills/firstmate/` or into a code check with a test, builds the checks the `enforceable` entries propose, and switches the coverage check to the new files. Other brittle tests also wait for phase 2 or later tasks: tests that hard-code option counts or source line numbers, the `fm_strip_comments` helper in `bin/fm-config.sh` (about line 965) and its users in `bin/ci.sh`, and the single-file module copies in `tests/merge.test.sh`, `tests/lib/worker.sh`, `tests/stacking-binding.test.sh`, `tests/lib/binding-fixture.sh` and `tests/gate-names.test.sh`.
